# Data dictionary — Kabadiwala Connect seed datasets

**SIH PS 26229.** Generated by `gen/build.py`, seed `26229`. Window: 2024-08-31 → 2026-08-31 (prices), 2025-03-01 → 2026-08-31 (field activity). Re-running the generator reproduces byte-identical files; `MANIFEST.json` carries row counts and SHA-256 prefixes so a judge can verify that.

> **Provenance statement — say this out loud in the demo.** Every row here is **synthetic**. Prices are calibrated to publicly reported Indian scrap-market ranges and are illustrative, not audited market data. Recycler names, CPCB registration numbers and phone numbers are fabricated. No real person's data appears anywhere. The only non-synthetic asset in the project is the ~300-image field pilot set the team shoots and the two collector interviews.

## Design decisions worth defending

**The formal/informal spread varies structurally by category.** It is not a flat markup, because the whole economic argument depends on *where* informal processing destroys value:

| Category | Mean spread | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Cable | 5.2% | Informal copper recovery is genuinely efficient — the platform's honest pitch here is safety and traceability, not money |
| Mixed plastic | 10.4% | Low value, high volume |
| LCD/LED panel | 19.1% | Indium and backlight handling need equipment |
| Battery (Li-ion) | 19.5% | Lithium and cobalt are lost entirely to backyard routes |
| CRT | 19.4% | Informal buyers barely want leaded glass; EPR obligations give formal recyclers a reason to pay |
| Motor & magnet | 21.6% | Neodymium magnets are simply not recovered informally |
| PCB | 25.6% | Acid leaching recovers some gold and destroys tantalum and everything else |

If a judge asks "why would a collector switch for 5% on cable?" — they wouldn't, and you should say so. The platform wins on PCBs, batteries, motors and CRTs, and the cable trade rides along because the collector is already in the app.

**Anomalies are labelled, not hidden.** 4.3% of transactions carry `is_anomaly = true` with one of four `anomaly_type` values: `price_out_of_band`, `weight_value_mismatch`, `impossible_geography`, `duplicate_photo`. The duplicate-photo rows genuinely reuse another lot's `image_ref`, so a perceptual-hash check actually finds them. **Never feed `is_anomaly` or `anomaly_type` to a model as a feature** — they are ground-truth labels for evaluating the detector.

**Lapsed-authorisation trades are in the data on purpose.** 2.7% of historical transactions went to a recycler whose authorisation had expired or was suspended (`recycler_authorised_at_txn = false`). This is what the admin compliance view exists to flag, and it demonstrates that the matching engine's exclusion rule is doing something real.

**35.9% of handovers were captured offline** (`device_offline_at_capture`), with a median sync lag of about 10 hours and a tail out to five days. That column is the evidence for the offline-first claim.

**A lot is a consolidated batch, not one item.** Collectors accumulate over several days and sell in bulk, so `item_count` records how many pieces make up the lot and `weight_kg` is the batch total.

## Column reference

### material_taxonomy.csv
`material_code` (join key, e.g. `PCB-RAM`) · `material_category` · `sub_category` · `unit` (kg) · `base_informal_rate_inr_per_kg` · `formal_premium_pct` · `price_volatility` · `price_family` (which commodity index the price tracks: copper / precious / battery / polymer / indium / glass) · `primary_hazard` · `informal_processing_risk` (plain-language hazard, drives the safety module) · `{lithium,cobalt,neodymium,tantalum,gallium,indium}_g_per_kg` (recoverable via the formal route) · `critical_materials_lost_informal`.

### price_history.csv
`price_id` · `date` · `material_code` · `material_category` · `sub_category` · `city` · `unit` · `buying_price_informal` (₹/kg an informal aggregator pays) · `quoted_price_formal` (₹/kg an authorised recycler offers) · `spread_pct` · `market_range_low` / `market_range_high` · `benchmark_recycler_id` · `source`.

Series construction: `base_rate × city_multiplier × commodity_index(t) × seasonal(t) × noise`. The commodity index is a drifting AR(1) with two visible market corrections at roughly 34% and 71% through the window. Seasonality: Diwali clear-out surge (Oct–Nov, +6%), monsoon softening (Jun–Aug, −4%), financial year-end office disposal (Mar–Apr, +2%). City multipliers: Mumbai 1.06, Pune 1.03, Pimpri-Chinchwad 1.02, Nashik 0.99, Nagpur 0.97, Aurangabad 0.96.

**Suitable for:** price-trend charts, a 7/30-day forecast baseline, and detecting out-of-band quotes. **Not suitable for:** any claim about real market prices on a specific date.

### price_board_current.csv
`material_code` · `city` · category/sub-category · current informal and formal price · `spread_pct` · `chg_7d_pct` · `chg_30d_pct` · `trend_7d` (up/down/flat) · `as_of_date`. This is the table the collector price board and its audio read-out consume.

### recyclers.csv
`recycler_id` · `name` · `facility_type` (authorised_recycler / authorised_dismantler / authorised_aggregator) · `city` · `industrial_estate` · `lat` / `lng` · `materials_accepted` (pipe-delimited categories) · `cpcb_registration_no` · `authorisation_status` (active 49, expiring_soon 10, expired 9, suspended 7) · `authorisation_valid_till` · `contact_phone` · `offered_rate_multiplier` (facility-level premium/discount on the city price) · `pickup_available` · `min_lot_weight_kg` · `service_area_radius_km` · `avg_settlement_hours` · `rating` · `capacity_tonnes_per_month` · `verified_on` · `is_synthetic`.

Facilities are clustered on real MIDC industrial estates (Bhosari, Chakan, Ranjangaon, Taloja, Mahape, Satpur, Ambad, Butibori, Hingna, Waluj, Shendra) with a few kilometres of scatter.

### collectors.csv
`collector_id` · `display_name` · `preferred_language` (mr 62% / hi 30% / other 8%) · `home_city` · `operating_areas` · `device_tier` (entry / mid / feature_android) · `literacy_tier` (non_reader 27% / numerals_only 44% / functional 29%) · `active_days_per_month` · `joined_on` · `onboarded_by` · `pii_minimised`.

**Deliberately not collected:** Aadhaar or any government ID, home address, caste, religion, household size, total income, family details. This is a design choice the problem statement explicitly asks for — put it on a slide.

### lots.csv
`lot_id` · `collector_id` · `created_at` · `material_category` / `sub_category` / `material_code` · `item_count` · `description_voice_transcript` (code-mixed Marathi/Hindi, e.g. *"18 kilo tambe waayar"*) · `transcript_language` · `input_method` (voice 70% / icon_keypad 24% / assisted 6%) · `image_ref` · `weight_kg` · `weight_source` (spring_balance / platform_scale / estimated) · `condition` · `source_type` · `collection_city` / `collection_area` / `collection_lat` / `collection_lng` · `estimated_value_informal` · `estimated_value_formal` · `predicted_category` · `prediction_confidence` · `prediction_accepted_by_user` · `created_offline`.

`predicted_category` and `prediction_confidence` come from the **calibrated classifier stub**, not a trained model. Per-category accuracy: CRT 0.95, Cable 0.93, Battery 0.88, Mixed plastic 0.84, LCD 0.82, Motor 0.80, **PCB 0.71** — PCB is deliberately weakest because separating high-grade from low-grade board is genuinely hard from a photo. Wrong predictions carry lower confidence (~0.61) than right ones (~0.88), which is what makes a confidence threshold meaningful in the UI.

### transactions.csv
`txn_id` · `lot_id` · `lot_image_ref` · `collector_id` · `recycler_id` · material fields · `weight_kg` (collector's figure) · `weight_verified_kg` (recycler's scale) · `quoted_price` · `final_price` · `informal_benchmark_value` (what the same lot would have fetched informally that day — the counterfactual the whole pitch rests on) · collection and handover coordinates · `handover_distance_km` · `quoted_at` / `handed_over_at` / `confirmed_at` / `settled_at` · `payment_mode` (cash 68% / upi 32%) · `payment_status` · `txn_status` (settled 70%, confirmed 9%, handed_over 7%, matched 6%, quoted 5%, cancelled 3%) · `pickup_by_recycler` · `recycler_authorisation_at_txn` · `recycler_authorised_at_txn` · `is_anomaly` · `anomaly_type`.

### traceability.csv
`trace_id` · `lot_id` · `txn_id` · `handover_ref` (unique, human-speakable `KC-XXXXXX`; alphabet excludes 0/O/1/I/5/S/2/Z/8/B so a non-reader can say it aloud without ambiguity) · `photo_refs` · `photo_reused_from_other_lot` · `scale_photo_ref` (the weighing-scale photo — the trust anchor for weight disputes) · `weight_kg` · `gps_lat` / `gps_lng` / `gps_accuracy_m` · `captured_at` · `device_offline_at_capture` · `synced_at` · `sync_lag_minutes` · `recycler_confirmed_at` · `confirmation_method` (qr_scan 44% / code_entry 38% / spoken_code 18%) · `downstream_status` (awaiting_confirmation → received_at_facility → segregated → sent_for_recovery → recovery_complete) · `epr_credit_reference`.

### ml_image_index.csv
`image_id` · `image_ref` · `label_source` · `usable_for_training` · category fields · `weight_kg` · `city` · `month` · `lighting` · `background` · `hand_for_scale` · `split` (70/15/15).

**Read this honestly:** 300 rows are `field_capture_pilot` — real photos the team shoots, the only rows with `usable_for_training = true`. The other 2,100 are `procedural_placeholder`, present so the UI is fully populated and so the index schema is demonstrable. **Do not train a model on the placeholders and do not claim you did.** The defensible position in front of judges is: here is our 300-image pilot set, here is the stub's confusion matrix, here is what productionising a MobileNetV3 / EfficientNet-Lite classifier would need (roughly 3–5k labelled images per category, multi-city, multi-season).

### collector_earnings.csv
Per-collector rollup over the 18-month window: `total_lots_transacted` · `total_weight_kg` · `gross_earnings_platform_inr` · `informal_benchmark_inr` · `earnings_paid_inr` · `earnings_pending_inr` · `uplift_vs_informal_inr` · `uplift_pct`. Cancelled transactions are excluded.

Median active collector: **17 lots, ~515 kg, ~₹3,800/month of e-waste income, 15.4% above the informal benchmark** (10th percentile 8.8%, 90th 24.0%). Treat this as a supplementary income stream, not the collector's whole livelihood — that framing is both true and more persuasive than overclaiming.

### unit_economics.csv
Per category: `lots` · `total_weight_kg` · `informal_value_inr` · `platform_value_inr` · `uplift_inr` · `uplift_pct` · `avg_lot_weight_kg` · `informal_rate_inr_per_kg` · `platform_rate_inr_per_kg` · `platform_fee_inr_at_1_75pct` · `collector_fee_inr` (zero, always — the fee is billed to the recycler; charging the collector kills adoption and you should say that on the slide).

### impact_summary.csv
Per sub-category: `weight_formalised_kg` and grams of lithium, cobalt, neodymium, tantalum, gallium and indium routed to formal recovery instead of backyard processing, plus `open_burning_events_avoided` (modelled at 55% of cable lots and 12% of others — a modelled estimate, label it as one).

Across the window: **~386 tonnes formalised**, ~125 kg lithium, ~245 kg cobalt, ~425 kg neodymium, ~22 kg tantalum, ~3 kg indium.

---

## Known limitations — put these on a slide before a judge finds them

1. Prices are synthetic and calibrated, not observed. No claim about any specific date is defensible.
2. Only 300 images are real. The classifier in the demo is a calibrated stub behind a real model interface (`services/api/ml/classifier.py`), not a trained network.
3. The anomaly detector is rule-based (z-score against the local price band, weight-value ratio, geo-velocity, perceptual-hash duplicates). No learned model, and it is labelled as such in the UI.
4. Six Maharashtra cities only. Nothing here generalises to another state without regeneration.
5. Collector behaviour is drawn from a Pareto activity distribution, not observed field logs. The two required field interviews are what ground this — do them.
6. `open_burning_events_avoided` and the EPR credit references are modelled illustrations, not measurements.
